segments.text: Your onboarding sequence has great click
rates, but here is the uncomfortable
question. Would those users have
activated anyway?
Clicks prove people read an email. They
do not prove it changed what they did.
The way to find out is a holdout group.
In this video, how to run one.
First, the idea.
It is simple.
Take new users as they sign up and split
them randomly. Most of them, say 90% get
the onboarding sequence as normal. A
small group gets nothing extra. They
still get essential emails like
verification and receipts. After a few
weeks, compare what the two groups did.
Did they activate? Are they still
around? Did they pay?
Next, reading the results.
Here is an illustrative result. 42% of
users who got the sequence activated
within 14 days, 36% of the holdout did
too. So the sequence added about six
points, not 42. That is the email's real
effect, and it is the number to compare
when you rewrite the sequence.
Two warnings. You need enough people. A
holdout of a few dozen tells you
nothing. So wait until each group has
hundreds
and decide what you are measuring before
you start so you are not tempted to pick
whichever number looks best.
Finally, running it fairly.
Five rules. Assign randomly at sign up,
never by hand. Essential emails like
verification, resets, and receipts go to
everyone. Keep the holdout small and
time limited because those users are
missing something you believe helps.
Measure behavior like activation and
retention, not email clicks. And write
down the result, then end the test.
Run it again when you change the
sequence significantly.
Holdouts are not only for onboarding.
They work for reengagement campaigns,
trial ending reminders, and even
newsletters.
Start with the email you believe matters
most. It is often the one where the
answer surprises you.
A random holdout shows what email really
changes. Next, is your list growing or
just churning?
